title: Given a single positive integer N, draw a flowchart to print all even integers between 1 and N inclusive. Start, read N, initialize i = 2, loop while i <= N doing print i and i = i + 2, End. Alternatively loop i from 1 to N and print i only when i % 2 == 0. Input: 10, Expected Output: 2 4 6 8 10.
shortTitle: Print Even Numbers — print all even integers between 1 and N

s1_definition.profdef: This problem generates the even numbers up to N. The efficient approach starts a counter at two and steps by two, printing each value while it stays within N, so it only ever touches even numbers. The alternative walks every integer and filters with a modulo test. The stepping approach is preferred because it does half the iterations and performs no conditional check per element.

The system lists two, four, six, eight, and ten for N equal to ten, stepping two at a time so it never wastes time looking at the odd ones.
s1_definition.oneliner: Print evens by starting at two and stepping by two up to N, which is more efficient than walking all numbers and filtering with a modulo test.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem generates the even numbers up to N. The efficient approach starts a counter at two and steps by two, printing each value while it stays within N, so it only ever touches even numbers. The alternative walks every integer and filters with a modulo test. The stepping approach is preferred because it does half the iterations and performs no conditional check per element.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India schedules an audit of accounts whose sequence numbers are even, perhaps every second account in a numbered list, up to account number N. The system lists two, four, six, eight, and ten for N equal to ten, stepping two at a time so it never wastes time looking at the odd ones.

**One line to remember:** Print evens by starting at two and stepping by two up to N, which is more efficient than walking all numbers and filtering with a modulo test.

sections.s2_technical:
The stepping approach initializes a counter i to two, then loops while i is less than or equal to N, printing i and increasing i by two each time. Because it begins at the first even number and advances in steps of two, every value it produces is even and it performs exactly N over two iterations. There is no per-element modulo test, which makes it both faster and simpler to reason about.

The alternative approach loops i from one to N and prints i only when i modulo two equals zero. This does twice as many iterations and a modulo test on each, so it is less efficient, but it is a useful illustration of the filter pattern and is handy when the step is not a simple constant. I would choose the stepping version for pure even-number generation and reserve the filter version for cases where the selection rule is more complex than a fixed stride.

In a banking batch the output is usually collected rather than printed one number at a time, so I accumulate the even values into a list and return it, which is easier to test and to feed downstream. I validate that N is at least one, and I handle the case where N is less than two by simply producing an empty result, because there are no even numbers in that range. A senior nuance is that for very large N you would stream the values rather than materialize a huge list, but the stepping loop is the same either way, and collecting into a list keeps the demo testable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India audits every even-numbered account up to a cutoff N. We must generate the even numbers from two to N. This is exactly the start-at-two, step-by-two loop.

Problem 2 — Walking every number and testing each with modulo would double the work for no benefit. This is exactly why the stepping approach, which touches only even numbers, is preferred.

Problem 3 — The result must be easy to test and pass downstream, not just printed. This is exactly why we collect the evens into a list and return it.

Our mini-project builds an `EvenLister` with an `evensUpTo(int n)` method returning a list and an `EvenNumbersDemo` runnable that prints two, four, six, eight, ten for N equal to ten.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: N = 10.

Step 1 — The counter i is initialized to two, the first even number, and an empty result list is created.

Step 2 — The loop checks two <= ten, true, adds two to the list, and advances i to four.

Step 3 — Subsequent iterations add four, six, eight, and ten, advancing i to twelve after adding ten.

Step 4 — The check twelve <= ten is false, so the loop stops. The list now holds two, four, six, eight, ten.

Step 5 — The list is returned and logged as the even account numbers to audit. If N had been one, the first check two <= one would be false and the result would be an empty list, which is correct because there are no even numbers in that range.

Final output:

```
2026-11-01 00:00:00 [INFO] Even account numbers to audit up to 10: [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: N = 10
    │
    ▼
  i = 2, result = []
    │
    ▼
  while i <= N (step 2):
    i=2 → add 2
    i=4 → add 4
    i=6 → add 6
    i=8 → add 8
    i=10 → add 10
    │ i=12 → 12<=10 false → stop
    ▼
  Output: [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Even Generation by Stride ═══

  ┌─ Principles ─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: lister only produces even numbers         │
  │  Start 2, step 2 → O(N/2), no per-item modulo │
  │  n<2 → empty list (safe boundary)             │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │          EvenLister          │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + evensUpTo(n:int): List<Int>│ throws IllegalArgumentException
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for evensUpTo(n):
    Pre:  n >= 1
    Post: returns [2,4,...] up to n (empty if n < 2)
    Throws: IllegalArgumentException on n < 1

  Call Chain:
  1. evensUpTo(10)
  2.   i=2; step 2 while i<=10
  3.   add 2,4,6,8,10
  4.   return list
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Printing the even numbers up to N can be done two ways, and the choice shows whether you think about efficiency. The efficient way starts a counter at two and steps it by two, printing each value while it stays within N, so it only ever touches even numbers and does about N over two iterations with no test per element. The alternative walks every integer from one to N and prints only those where the number modulo two is zero, which does twice the iterations and a modulo check each time. For N equal to ten both produce two, four, six, eight, ten, but the stepping approach is cleaner and faster.

I prefer the stepping approach for straightforward even generation and reserve the filter approach for when the selection rule is more complex than a fixed stride. I also handle the boundary where N is less than two by returning nothing, because there are no even numbers in that range, and in real code I collect the values into a list and return it rather than printing them one at a time, because a returned collection is far easier to test and to pass to the next stage.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I used this to build an audit worklist of even-numbered accounts up to a cutoff. I wrote an EvenLister whose evensUpTo method starts at two and steps by two, collecting the results into a list, and validates that N is positive. For a cutoff of ten it produced two, four, six, eight, and ten, and a cutoff below two produced an empty list cleanly. The lesson I emphasize is that even a simple generation task rewards picking the stride loop over the filter loop, because it halves the work and removes a conditional, and returning a collection instead of printing makes it production-ready.
